content: The Yuzpe Regimen is an emergency contraceptive method that involves the use of a combination of estrogen and progestogen hormones. It must be initiated within 72 hours of unprotected sexual intercourse to reduce the risk of pregnancy. This method has largely been replaced by a progestogen-only hormonal regimen due to its improved efficacy and reduced side effects. The Yuzpe method was developed by Dr. A. Albert Yuzpe, a Canadian professor, who first published studies on its safety and effectiveness in 1974. This regimen works by administering two doses of combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) containing estrogen and progestogen, taken 12 hours apart. The effectiveness of the method is highest when initiated as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse. Its efficacy significantly decreases if started more than 72 hours after intercourse. In contrast, emergency intrauterine device (IUD) insertion is highly effective for up to five days after ovulation, which may extend beyond five days after the unprotected sexual encounter. The specific hormone doses in the Yuzpe Regimen typically consist of two tablets, each containing 50 µg of ethinyl estradiol and 250 µg of levonorgestrel, followed by a second identical dose 12 hours later. Depending on the brand of COCPs used, the number of pills per dose may vary from 2 to 5. For individuals taking medications that enhance liver metabolism (e.g., rifamycin or certain anticonvulsants), higher doses of hormones may be required, or an IUD may be a more suitable alternative. It is important to note that the Yuzpe Regimen is not 100% effective in preventing pregnancy. Additionally, while the hormones may cause the next menstrual period to arrive a few days earlier or later than expected, a pregnancy test is recommended if the period is delayed by more than three days. This method does not provide protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The World Health Organization (WHO) later investigated the use of progestogen-only emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), which demonstrated greater efficacy and fewer side effects compared to the Yuzpe Regimen. As a result, progestogen-only ECPs have largely replaced the Yuzpe method. A single dose of 100 mg mifepristone has also been shown to be more effective than the Yuzpe Regimen. The Yuzpe Regimen is associated with some temporary side effects, which are generally mild. These include: Nausea and/or vomiting Breast tenderness Irregular bleeding Headache or dizziness If vomiting occurs within three hours of taking a dose, it is possible that insufficient hormones were absorbed, and an additional dose should be taken. Take the pills with food. If prone to nausea, consider taking an antiemetic such as Dramamine or Bonine one hour before the pills (though this is not mandatory). Schedule the second dose to be taken before bedtime. Many commonly available combined oral contraceptive pills can be used for the Yuzpe Regimen, even though they are not specifically labeled for this purpose. Such off-label use of approved medications is both legal and common in medical practice in the United States. In February 1997, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) officially declared the emergency contraceptive use of certain birth control pills, following the Yuzpe Regimen, to be safe and effective. However, dedicated Yuzpe Regimen products, such as Preven in the U.S. and Schering-PC4 in the U.K., were discontinued after the introduction of progestogen-only emergency contraceptive pills, such as Plan B in the U.S. and Levonelle in the U.K.
